title: Οὐρὰ καὶ μέλη ὄφεως
titleEn: The Tail and the Members of a Snake
part: The Tail and the Members of a Snake (Chambry 288 · Perry 362)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 288 (= Perry 362). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Οὐρά ποτε ὄφεως ἠξίου πρώτη προάγειν καὶ βαδίζειν.
sentences.tr: Oura pote opheōs ēxiou prōtē proagein kai badizein.
sentences.l: A snake's tail once claimed the right, as the first, to lead the way and to walk.
sentences.n: ἀξιόω is to think a thing one's due and so to demand it; the imperfect ἠξίου sets the claim going rather than settling it. πρώτη is a predicate nominative agreeing with the tail — she is to be the one in front.

sentences.t: Τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ μέλη ἔλεγον· « Πῶς χωρὶς ὀμμάτων καὶ ῥινὸς ἡμᾶς ἄξεις, ὡς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ζῷα ; »
sentences.tr: Ta de loipa melē elegon· « Pōs chōris ommatōn kai rhinos hēmas axeis, hōs kai ta loipa zōia ; »
sentences.l: And the remaining members said: « How, without eyes and nose, will you lead us, as the other animals too? »
sentences.i: And the other members said: « Without eyes or a nose, how will you lead us, the way the rest of the animals are led? »
sentences.n: μέλη are the limbs or members of a body; a snake has none in the usual sense, and the fable's comedy begins there. The clause ὡς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ζῷα has no verb of its own, and the one to be understood could be either 'are led' or 'do' — the Greek leaves it open, and the idiomatic line has to choose.

sentences.t: Ταύτην δὲ οὐκ ἔπειθον, ἕως τὸ φρονοῦν ἐνικήθη.
sentences.tr: Tautēn de ouk epeithon, heōs to phronoun enikēthē.
sentences.l: But her they were not persuading, until the thinking part was defeated.
sentences.i: But they could not persuade her, until at last the part that had the sense was overruled.
sentences.n: ἔπειθον is a conative imperfect — they were trying to persuade, and failing; the aorist would have reported success. τὸ φρονοῦν is a participle with the article doing duty as a noun, 'the thing that has sense', i.e. the head.

sentences.t: Ἡ οὐρὰ δὲ ἦρχε καὶ ἦγε, σύρουσα τυφλὴ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα, ἕως, εἰς βάραθρον πετρῶν ἐνεχθείσης, ⟨ὁ ὄφις⟩ τὴν ῥάχιν καὶ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα ἐπλήγη.
sentences.tr: Hē oura de ērche kai ēge, syrousa typhlē pan to sōma, heōs, eis barathron petrōn enechtheisēs, ⟨ho ophis⟩ tēn rhachin kai pan to sōma eplēgē.
sentences.l: And the tail ruled and led, dragging, blind, the whole body, until, she having been carried into a pit of rocks, ⟨the snake⟩ was struck on the spine and over the whole body.
sentences.i: So the tail took command and led, blind, dragging the whole body after it, until she was carried over into a rocky pit and the snake was battered on its spine and over its whole body.
sentences.n: The genitive absolute ἐνεχθείσης has no expressed subject: the feminine ending alone tells the reader it is the tail. ⟨ὁ ὄφις⟩ is Chambry's own supplement — angle brackets are words he adds — and the literal line keeps them. τὴν ῥάχιν καὶ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα are accusatives of respect with the passive ἐπλήγη: struck as to the spine, as to the whole body.

sentences.t: Σαίνουσα δὲ ἱκέτευε τὴν κεφαλὴν λέγουσα· « Σῶσον ἡμᾶς, εἰ θέλεις, δέσποινα· τῆς γὰρ κακῆς ἔριδος ἐπειράθην. »
sentences.tr: Sainousa de hiketeue tēn kephalēn legousa· « Sōson hēmas, ei theleis, despoina· tēs gar kakēs eridos epeirathēn. »
sentences.l: And fawning she was entreating the head, saying: « Save us, if you will, mistress; for I have made trial of the evil strife. »
sentences.i: And fawning on the head she begged her: « Save us, if you will, mistress — I have had my trial of this evil strife. »
sentences.n: σαίνω is the dog's word for wagging the tail in submission, which is exactly what the tail is now reduced to doing. πειράομαι takes the genitive of what one makes trial of; ἐπειράθην is an aorist, and an English perfect carries it best here. δέσποινα is the mistress of a household — the head is granted the rank the tail had wanted.

sentences.t: Ἄνδρας δολίους καὶ κακοὺς καὶ τοῖς δεσπόταις ἐπανισταμένους ὁ μῦθος ἐλέγχει.
sentences.tr: Andras dolious kai kakous kai tois despotais epanistamenous ho mythos elenchei.
sentences.l: Men treacherous and wicked and rising up against their masters the fable exposes.
sentences.i: The fable exposes men who are treacherous and wicked and who rise up against their masters.
sentences.n: A closing formula met elsewhere in the collection, ὁ μῦθος ἐλέγχει (as at fable 93 and fable 227): ἐλέγχω is the courtroom word, to put a man to the proof and so show him up. ἐπανίσταμαι takes the dative of those risen against, and δεσπόταις answers the δέσποινα the tail was calling on a line earlier.
